document_check.note: Yamada Y, Shinkawa K, Nemoto M, Nemoto K, Arai T. A mobile application using automatic speech analysis for classifying Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment. Computer Speech & Language 81 (2023) 101514, doi 10.1016/j.csl.2023.101514. The file is 1-s2.0-S0885230823000335-main.pdf, which is the summaries.md title of Paper 60. There are 114 participants (43 CN, 46 MCI, 25 AD), recorded with a voice application on an iPad Air 2. Table 6 and the text on p. 8 report the RBF-SVM result for MCI versus CN: accuracy 87.6%, sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 87.2%. This matches the citation.

cited_result: Nested leave-one-out classification of clinically diagnosed MCI (n=46) versus cognitively normal (n=43) participants. The inputs are 92 speech features extracted automatically from recordings made with a voice application on an iPad Air 2 tablet. The RBF-kernel SVM reaches accuracy 87.6%, sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 87.2% and F1 87.1% (Table 6; text p. 8).
tool_reason: The cited result is the discrimination (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity) of a machine-learning classifier (SVM on speech features) that separates MCI from cognitively normal participants. That is a diagnostic prediction-model question, so PROBAST applies, with the PROBAST+AI considerations.

domains.rationale: The patients were psychiatry outpatients who already had a diagnosis of AD or MCI. The controls were their spouses and community volunteers, age-matched to the patients. This is a two-gate (diagnostic case-control) design with no consecutive or random sampling frame, and the paper does not report how many people were screened or excluded. MCI was restricted to AD-type MCI meeting CDR and ADNI-style cut-offs, and non-AD MCI was excluded. Together these remove the ambiguous presentations a screening tool would meet.

signalling.question: 1.1 Were appropriate data sources used?
signalling.quote: We recruited outpatients from the Department of Psychiatry, University of Tsukuba Hospital, along with their spouses, and other participants either through local recruiting agencies or community advertisements in Ibaraki, Japan. [p. 2]; CN participants were then age-matched with the patients. [p. 3]

signalling.question: 1.2 Were all inclusions and exclusions of participants appropriate?
signalling.quote: Patients were excluded if they had diagnoses of non-AD dementia (dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia, vascular dementia, etc.), non-AD MCI, or other serious diseases or disabilities that would interfere with the collection of speech data.

domains.rationale: Every participant answered the same prerecorded questions on the same tablet in the same room. The 92 features were extracted automatically (ASR, voice activity detection, signal-processing libraries), so extraction did not depend on knowing the diagnosis. The features would be available at the intended time of use. There are two minor departures: the experimenter repeated instructions when needed, and caregivers sat behind the partition for a few dementia patients. The caregivers did not attend any participant in the MCI versus CN comparison.

domains.rationale: MCI was defined by the NIA-AA core clinical criteria plus CDR and ADNI-style MMSE and logical-memory criteria. Two dementia psychiatrists confirmed each diagnosis while blind to the speech analysis, and the CN group was defined with the same instruments. No speech feature enters the outcome definition, although the app's subtraction task shares content with the MMSE serial sevens. The paper does not report the interval between clinical assessment and recording. The diagnoses are clinical, without biomarkers, as the authors acknowledge; for a clinically defined MCI target this is not judged a source of bias.

signalling.quote: the diagnoses of AD, MCI, and CN were confirmed by two psychiatrists (authors T. A. and K. N.), who are experts in dementia and were blind to the results of the speech data analysis. For this confirmation, they examined each case in terms of the clinical record and the cognitive and clinical measures.

signalling.quote: clinical criteria for MCI (Albert et al., 2011): (i) cognitive concern by the subject, an informant, or a clinician; (ii) impairment in one or more cognitive domains; (iii) essentially normal functional activities; and (iv) absence of dementia.

domains.rationale: For MCI versus CN there are 46 participants with the outcome against 92 candidate features, about 0.5 events per candidate predictor (about 20 features selected per fold). Several parts of the validation are appropriate: nested leave-one-out at the participant level, LASSO feature selection and grid-search tuning in the inner loop, and class weights tuned for a near-balanced sample. However, six algorithms were compared on the outer-loop results and only the best is reported (RBF SVM 87.6%; the other five 49.4% to 85.4%). That choice adds optimism the nested design does not remove. The paper does not say whether scaling and imputation were fitted within folds. Performance is reported as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 only, with no AUC, calibration or confidence interval. The permutation test covers only the three-class accuracy. The MCI group had fewer women than the CN group (39% vs 65%), and the leading MCI features are pitch variation and MFCC variances, voice features that may differ by sex; no adjustment for sex is reported. There is no external validation.

applicability.rationale: The participants are psychiatry outpatients with AD-type MCI and age-matched spouse or community controls, all Japanese speakers at one university hospital. Non-AD MCI was excluded.

Recordings were made in a quiet laboratory room, with a hidden experimenter who re-instructed participants when needed. The intended use is self-administered screening, and the authors acknowledge the laboratory setting as a limitation.
MCI is defined clinically by NIA-AA criteria, which is the target of a screening tool. There is no biomarker confirmation.

overall_rationale: Two domains are high. Domain 1: two-gate recruitment of diagnosed outpatients against age-matched spouse and community controls, with non-AD MCI excluded. Domain 4: 46 events against 92 candidate features, the best of six algorithms reported from the outer-loop results, no AUC, calibration or confidence interval, sex imbalance not addressed, and internal validation only. Domains 2 and 3 are low.
